episode_title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH

stories.topic: The Restaurant That Could Never Have the Right Number of Doors
stories.summary: A friend of Amit's ran a restaurant in Bangalore. The fire department told him he needed multiple entrances. The excise department told him he could have only one, so that it could track alcohol going in and out. Officials from all of these departments took bribes from him, whatever number of doors he had.
stories.insight: This is rent-seeking in miniature. When the state controls permissions and its rules contradict each other, compliance becomes impossible, and that impossibility is what officials can charge for.
stories.quote: the fire department said you have to have multiple entrances, and the excise department said you can only have one entrance because we want to track alcohol going in and out. And all of them are taking bribes from the poor guy, you know, no matter how many doors he has.

stories.summary: Amit was a professional poker player, so he watched this from the inside. Sheldon Adelson owned physical casinos, including the Sands and the Venetian. He was a big funder of the Republican Party and spent years lobbying to keep online poker banned, which made him widely hated among poker professionals. He believed online poker threatened his casinos. Amit points out the irony: it didn't. The overall gambling ecosystem grew, and live casinos were not hurt.
stories.insight: Special interests lobby based on what they believe will protect them, not on what is true. Consumers can lose out even when the threat the lobbyist fears is imaginary.
stories.quote: Actually, it is kinda ironic that it really wasn't. It's just that the ecosystem of gambling expanded when online poker came in. It didn't hurt the live casinos. But he thought it would hurt the live casinos.

stories.topic: Why Raees Gets Public Choice Wrong
stories.summary: Amit set Ajay a quiz: what does Shah Rukh Khan's film Raees have to do with public choice theory? In the film, SRK plays a macho bootlegger in Gujarat, where alcohol is banned. He tries to stop a politician who is leading a Darubandi Yatra, a rally demanding that alcohol be banned. Amit says this makes no sense. Under Bruce Yandle's 'bootleggers and Baptists' idea, the prohibitionist and the bootlegger are on the same side: the Baptist gets alcohol banned, and the bootlegger then profits by selling it.
stories.insight: Moral crusaders and the people who profit from a ban are often quiet allies. Before trusting a pious-sounding regulation, ask who gains from it.
stories.quote: actually the bootlegger and the politician who wants alcohol banned, their interests are the same, they're on the same side.

stories.summary: In a Housefull Economics column, Amit wrote about the film Newton. Rajkummar Rao plays an election officer who sets up polling booths in Chhattisgarh and tries to teach people their civic duty. The voters who turn up have no interest in who is on the ballot; they came only because they had to. Amit says that, unlike Raees, this film understands the economics: it shows Anthony Downs's idea of rational ignorance.
stories.insight: Voter indifference is not stupidity. It is a reasonable response when one vote almost never changes the outcome. A good film can teach an economic idea better than a lecture.
stories.quote: They don't care who's on the ballot. They don't give a shit. They've shown up because they had to show up.

stories.topic: The Election Lost by One Vote
stories.summary: Amit once said on The Seen and the Unseen that a single vote never decides an election. A listener corrected him: a local election in India had been decided by exactly one vote, and the losing candidate's wife had not gone to vote.
stories.insight: Rational ignorance holds for the typical voter. But rare cases exist where a single vote really does decide the result, and sometimes they happen close to home.
stories.quote: there was some local election in India which was decided by one vote, and the loser's wife hadn't gone to vote. So which is like kindly if your spouse is in an election, kindly vote.

stories.topic: How India Nearly Got Proportional Representation
stories.summary: In Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode with Jayaprakash Narayan, JP describes how he almost got proportional representation adopted. He had friends in high places and spoke to the different parties, and when the UPA was in power all the principal players had nearly agreed. Then Sonia Gandhi said no, believing Congress would stay in power under first-past-the-post and that PR would hurt it. Amit notes the irony: under PR, the BJP would not be as dominant today and Congress would hold many more seats. When Amit raised PR with Pratap Bhanu Mehta, PBM said it would be an absolute disaster that would tear the country apart. These are two of the people Amit considers the tallest intellectuals in India, and they hold opposite views.
stories.insight: People who block a reform because they assume their power is permanent often end up harmed by that choice. And the design of an electoral system is genuinely contested, even among the wisest people.
stories.quote: Now the irony of that is that had proportional representation got through the BJP would not be so dominant today and the Congress would have many more seats than they do.

stories.topic: An Honest Father in the IAS
stories.summary: Before discussing bureaucrats, Amit mentions that his father was an IAS officer and a good man, 'unfortunately for me' perhaps a little too honest, or completely honest. He uses this to reject the lazy stereotype that all babus are corrupt. In his view most bureaucrats are essentially good people who are responding to the incentives in front of them.
stories.insight: Public choice theory is about systems, not villains. If outcomes are bad, look at the incentives before blaming the people.
stories.quote: he was a good man and by all means unfortunately for me perhaps a little too honest, or completely honest.

stories.topic: Germany Designed Its Constitution Against Another Hitler
stories.summary: Ajay has been strongly influenced by the history behind the modern German constitution. Hitler's Nazi party won the 1933 elections with something like 32% of the vote and went on to destroy the country (Amit adds: an entire continent). After the Second World War, Germany's central design goal was to build checks and balances so that a small, passionate base could never again install an extremist. After much debate, they chose proportional representation. Ajay says he is not an expert and offers this as a thought for listeners to explore.
stories.insight: Electoral rules are design choices made in response to specific dangers. First-past-the-post is not the natural or only form of democracy.
stories.quote: In Germany they felt that the number one problem was how to organize in a voting system such that you rule out the possibility of a small base which gets through, first past the post, and you get the Nazi party.

stories.topic: Vitalik Buterin and the Basti Auction
stories.summary: Ajay recalls the conversation he and Amit had with Vitalik Buterin. Vitalik argued that the core problem with voting systems is that it is too easy to bribe a person to vote against their own interest. Ajay says this happens all the time in India. Frontline electoral politics often means going to one community elder or one basti at a time, and whoever bids highest gets those votes. This greatly increases the influence of money in politics.
stories.insight: Elections can be bought wholesale. The weak point of democracy is not only the ignorant voter but also the voter who can be bought.
stories.quote: frontline electoral politics is a game of going to one community elder or one basti at a time and the highest bidder gets those votes.

stories.topic: No Shirt Worth Buying: Not Voting as a Signal
stories.summary: Amit once skipped an election because no party seemed worth voting for, and he didn't want to vote tactically for the least evil. Someone told him that if he hadn't voted, he had no right to an opinion on the result. He disagreed. If you go to a mall and every shirt is bad, you don't have to buy one, and your not buying tells the market there is a gap. Likewise, the many Indians who don't vote signal to political entrepreneurs that existing parties aren't meeting demand. Amit says the Aam Aadmi Party did exactly this. He did not like AAP and criticised them from the Anna movement days onward, but he calls them a remarkably successful piece of political entrepreneurship: they offered disaffected middle-class voters someone who looked like them and talked about corruption, which Amit notes is the first rallying cry of populist movements.
stories.insight: Staying away from the polls is also information. Gaps in the political market get filled by new entrants, for better or worse.
stories.quote: I am not obliged to buy a shirt. My not buying a shirt is a signal that there is a gap in the market and maybe that can be fulfilled.

recommendations.item: Public Choice – A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Recommended first in the reading list at the start of the episode; available as a free PDF from the IEA.
recommendations.reason: It was the first public choice book Amit read and his 'gateway drug' into the field. It is short enough to read in under an hour, and he calls it masterful.

recommendations.item: The Calculus of Consent
recommendations.creator: James M Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
recommendations.context: Named as the 1962 book that many regard as the start of public choice theory; returned to in the constitution chapter.
recommendations.reason: It is the founding text of the field. It also frames the constitution as the 'rules of the game', which ideally should rest on consensus.

recommendations.item: The Logic of Collective Action
recommendations.creator: Mancur Olson
recommendations.context: Part of the 1965 entry in Amit's reading list; Amit believes Ajay owns a first edition.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of 'concentrated benefits and diffuse costs', which explains why small organised interest groups beat the large unorganised public.

recommendations.item: An Economic Theory of Democracy
recommendations.creator: Anthony Downs
recommendations.context: Listed among the seminal books, then cited in the voting chapter.
recommendations.reason: Amit first learned about rational ignorance from this book: the idea that voters sensibly don't spend scarce attention on a vote that almost never decides anything.

recommendations.item: Books by William A Niskanen
recommendations.creator: William A Niskanen
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the reading list and again when discussing bureaucrats.
recommendations.reason: Amit says Niskanen has great books on the incentives of bureaucrats.

recommendations.item: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Rauch
recommendations.context: Recommended twice in the special interests chapter.
recommendations.reason: A scary read on how far special interests have captured the state in the US. India isn't there yet, Amit says, but could easily get there.

recommendations.item: Parkinson's Law
recommendations.creator: C Northcote Parkinson
recommendations.context: Brought up while discussing the incentives of bureaucrats.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a classic book of comedy that is also a public choice book. It covers how work expands to fill the time available, how officials multiply subordinates rather than rivals, and how they grow budgets and turf.

recommendations.item: Shruti Rajagopalan on our constitutional amendments
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: A video recommended in the constitution chapter.
recommendations.reason: It shows how often the Constitution has been amended. From Nehru onwards, governments have amended it whenever they wanted to do something unconstitutional. Amit calls it fantastic.

recommendations.item: Where Have All the Leaders Gone?
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Bloomberg Quint column, cited in the chapter on politicians.
recommendations.reason: It uses public choice to explain why the freedom struggle attracted people of principle, while today's centralised state attracts people who seek power.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The column Amit promises to link after saying that interventions in free markets redistribute from the poor to the rich.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the argument that protectionist measures such as banning FDI in retail transfer money from consumers to organised interest groups.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's remark that the strong-leader instinct to 'fix the price' doesn't work.
recommendations.reason: Further reading on why top-down fixes such as price controls backfire.

recommendations.item: Politics (limerick)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit recites it on air and calls it the first public choice limerick ever written; it was originally from his weekly Times of India limericks.
recommendations.reason: It captures the link between money and power in five lines.

recommendations.item: A Few Thoughts on Limericks
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The 'how to write limericks' link Amit promises after explaining that a limerick needs a syllable count as well as a rhyme scheme.
recommendations.reason: For readers who want to understand the craft, including the ideal 9-9-6-6-9 syllable count.

recommendations.item: Housefull Economics on Pragati
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's old Pragati column series that used Bollywood films to explain economic ideas; he wrote about Newton in it.
recommendations.reason: It explains economic concepts through films. Amit asks listeners whether they'd like a regular segment like it on the show.

recommendations.item: The Economics of Voting
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for the voting chapter.
recommendations.reason: Further reading on the voting questions discussed in the episode, such as rational ignorance and why people vote at all.

recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the story of the Bangalore restaurant owner trapped between the fire and excise departments.
recommendations.reason: A deeper look at how restaurant regulation in India works as an opportunity for rent-seeking.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan — Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Amit's eight-hour-plus episode, mentioned in the bureaucrats chapter.
recommendations.reason: Amit can hardly think of anyone he admires more for public service, intellectual integrity and honesty, though he considers KP Krishnan an outlier among bureaucrats.

recommendations.item: A Life in Indian Politics — Episode 149 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
recommendations.context: Cited in the discussion of first-past-the-post versus proportional representation.
recommendations.reason: Jayaprakash Narayan tells how India almost adopted proportional representation, until Sonia Gandhi said no.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pratap Bhanu Mehta

recommendations.item: The Anti-Defection Law — Episode 13 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
recommendations.context: Mentioned after the discussion of tactical voting and Arrow's theorem.

recommendations.item: Our Parliament and Our Democracy — Episode 253 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside the Barun Mitra episode as another place Amit discussed the anti-defection law.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant — Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah with Vitalik Buterin
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls the conversation he and Amit had with Vitalik in the voting chapter.
recommendations.reason: It contains Vitalik's insight that the core weakness of voting systems is how easy it is to bribe people to vote against their own interest.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh
recommendations.context: Cited in the constitution chapter.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma

recommendations.item: Understanding the State — Episode 25 of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay opens by recalling the earlier episode on the fundamental concept of a state; the show notes suggest watching it alongside this one.
recommendations.reason: It is the first part of the series on the state, of which public choice is the third.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? — Episode 26 of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled in the introduction as the episode on what a state should do and the difficulties of implementation.
recommendations.reason: It is the second part of the series, and this episode builds on it.

core_ideas.concept: Public Choice Theory: Governments Are People
core_ideas.explanation: Public choice applies economics, the study of how people respond to incentives under scarcity, to politics: politicians, bureaucrats, voters and the state. The government is not a benevolent being. It is made up of fallible people pursuing their own interests. Amit argues that there is no single aggregated 'public interest', because different people want different things. This matters especially in India, where he says the biggest religion is the religion of government, the 'Mai Baap Sarkar' expected to fix every problem.
core_ideas.quote: governments consist of people, right? And people respond to incentives.

core_ideas.concept: The State as a Community Holding a Monopoly on Violence
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cites Max Weber: the state is not a set of institutions but a community of people who achieve and maintain a monopoly of physical violence over a territory. Rule-bound, predictable institutions are something to aspire to, and countries achieve them to very different degrees. So we should ask what the people inside the state want and what they are trying to maximise. Amit adds a caution: even 'community' is too collective. Only individuals have values and interests, so keep thinking in terms of individuals.
core_ideas.quote: Max Weber's definition is the state is a community of people that achieve and maintain the monopoly of physical violence on a territory.

core_ideas.concept: Politicians Think Until the Next Election
core_ideas.explanation: A politician's main incentive is to get elected, so the time horizon is always the next election. A party leader is always facing some local election somewhere. Many good policies depend on counterintuitive truths: life is positive-sum, not zero-sum, and order emerges bottom-up in markets, languages and natural selection. People instinctively prefer a strong leader who will simply 'fix the price', so politicians cater to popular sentiment and neglect policies that only pay off in the long run. Amit adds the old cartoon of two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner as a reminder of the dangers of majority rule.
core_ideas.quote: This automatically means that a politician's time horizon is always a short term. It is the next election.

core_ideas.concept: Why Today's Politics Attracts Different People
core_ideas.explanation: Amit uses public choice to answer the lament that India no longer has leaders like its freedom fighters. Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and Rajaji were not competing for power, because power was not on offer, so politics attracted people driven by principle. Today's highly centralised state offers enormous power, so it attracts people who want power.
core_ideas.quote: If Nehru was alive today, I posit that he would be Pratap Bhanu Mehta. He would not be Narendra Modi

core_ideas.concept: Milton Friedman's Four Ways to Spend Money
core_ideas.explanation: Spending your own money on yourself makes you both economise and seek value. Spending your own money on a stranger makes you economise but not care much about value. Spending someone else's money on yourself makes you seek value but not economise. Spending someone else's money on someone else gives you no reason to do either, and that is government. Ajay adds PJ O'Rourke's line comparing giving money and power to politicians with giving whiskey and car keys to teenagers.
core_ideas.quote: And if I spend somebody else's money on somebody else, I will neither economize nor seek value. Right? This is the whole business of government

core_ideas.concept: Maybe the State Would Do More Good With Less Money
core_ideas.explanation: If you believe in the Mai Baap state, you will accept a higher tax-to-GDP ratio. If you are sceptical of how governments use coercion and spending, a lower ratio may be better. Ajay notes that this thought is almost absent among Indian economists, who generally favour bigger government.
core_ideas.quote: Maybe the Indian state would do more good if it had less money. And that's something which is really a thought that is not present amongst economists in India today.

core_ideas.concept: Rent-Seeking
core_ideas.explanation: Rent-seeking has nothing to do with renting out property. It is what happens when the state controls something or creates artificial scarcity and then profits from it. Amit's hypothetical: the government decides podcasters need a licence, renewable every six months, and he has to pay a bribe for each renewal.
core_ideas.quote: when the state has control of something or when it creates an artificial scarcity in something, it can then make a lot of money off that.

core_ideas.concept: Concentrated Benefits, Diffuse Costs
core_ideas.explanation: Politicians need money, and special interests supply it as an investment that will need a return, usually through policies that shield them from competition or redistribute wealth to them. The public doesn't notice because each person's loss is tiny and invisible, while the gain to the beneficiary is large. Amit's illustration: the government takes one rupee from everyone and hands it all to Ajay. Another example: small traders, who matter to some parties both as voters and as funders, push to keep FDI out of retail, and consumers quietly pay more for less.
core_ideas.quote: everybody who's losing one rupee, they don't even know they're losing one rupee. They don't even know where it's going. They don't care. So the costs are diffused.

core_ideas.concept: Market Interventions Redistribute From Poor to Rich
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's strong claim: whether it is protection from competition, a tariff on Chinese goods or a ban on FDI in retail, intervening in free markets takes money from the many and gives it to a well-organised few. Many regulations sound pious, so you have to dig into why they really exist.
core_ideas.quote: Which is why I say all interventions in free markets are redistributions from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.concept: Bootleggers and Baptists
core_ideas.explanation: This idea, coined by the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle, describes how a prohibition brings together the moralist (the Baptist, who says alcohol breaks families and must be banned) and the profiteer (the bootlegger, who sells the banned good). They look like enemies but want the same policy, and sometimes they literally work together.
core_ideas.quote: So the Baptist gets alcohol banned. So alcohol is banned, and then the bootlegger comes in

core_ideas.concept: Worse Than Lobbying Is a World Without It
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay complicates the anti-lobbying instinct. In London, New York or Tokyo, firms can openly criticise policy and lobby for their interests, which means power is spread out. In India, the rule of law has declined and regulators hold arbitrary power, so industry has been frightened into silence. In the same way, firms funding parties in exchange for favourable policy is bad, but a protection racket is worse: there, firms that don't pay face coercive state agencies. Amit adds that the deeper problem is a state with too much power to interfere in markets at all, which makes elections 'a battle to be the one legal mafia for five years'.
core_ideas.quote: the one thing worse than a world where private firms can lobby with the government and influence policy is one in which they cannot.

core_ideas.concept: Bureaucrats Protect and Expand Their Turf
core_ideas.explanation: Using Parkinson's Law and William A Niskanen, Amit describes bureaucratic incentives. Officials want more subordinates rather than rivals, bigger budgets and wider power. They resist any change with unpredictable consequences, which creates a status quo bias. Someone who would agree from the outside that a ministry should be abolished will defend it once inside.
core_ideas.quote: You are on a gravy train, you want that gravy train to continue as long as possible.

core_ideas.concept: The Administrative State
core_ideas.explanation: A healthy liberal democracy spreads power across the legislature, the judiciary and the executive, and also across journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs and citizens. In an administrative state, the legislature and judiciary stop acting as checks. Officials run the country, with ministers making the big calls and officers the small ones, and citizens become subjects. Ajay says this describes what India is becoming. Indians who apply Western ideas of liberal democracy misread their own situation. His remedy is more democracy: real checks and balances, and many sources of power outside government, so that officials feel the consequences when things go wrong.
core_ideas.quote: The administrative state is one in which power gets concentrated into the officials.

core_ideas.concept: Corruption Is More Than Suitcases of Cash
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay blames Bollywood for reducing corruption to suitcases of cash. His definition is broader: corruption is acting against the organisation's professional purpose for personal gain. That includes doing favours for friends and family, not enforcing the law against them, taking expedient career-boosting actions you don't believe in, maximising your own power, and laziness, meaning holding a civil servant's power while doing no work.
core_ideas.quote: I have grown to think of the word corruption as being doing things that are not aligned with the professional objectives of the organization for your own personal gain.

core_ideas.concept: When in Doubt, Ban It
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says Indian officials' urge to shut down parts of the economy no longer comes from Nehru-Mahalanobis-style central planning, which faded long ago. It comes from personal incentives: understanding cryptocurrency or complex derivatives is hard, so ban them. Closing restaurants at 10 pm prevents the occasional crime headline that could embarrass the official, who never sees the cost to the city's vitality and economy.
core_ideas.quote: doing good things that are good for the country are really not seen or rewarded, but getting into trouble will destroy your career.

core_ideas.concept: Rational Ignorance
core_ideas.explanation: Anthony Downs's idea: one vote almost never decides an election, and even if it did, it probably wouldn't change your life much. Time and attention are scarce, so it is rational not to study manifestos, track records and policy trade-offs.
core_ideas.quote: I want to spend that attention, I want to spend that time on things that affect me in the everyday. Right? Voting doesn't affect me in the everyday.

core_ideas.concept: Why People Vote Anyway
core_ideas.explanation: If voting rarely matters, why do people vote? One reason is a norm: you see yourself as a good citizen, just as you signal a left turn on an empty road. Another is tribal affiliation: voting is like wearing your club's red shirt to a Manchester United game.
core_ideas.quote: You vote for the same reason that you go to a Manchester United game.

core_ideas.concept: The State Cannot Demand Duties
core_ideas.explanation: Asked about a citizen's duty to vote, Ajay answers from first principles. The state has no right to demand duties of the people. Their fundamental right is to be left alone. He has never voted, because the cost-benefit calculation never made sense to him.
core_ideas.quote: So basics of political philosophy, the state has no right to ask duties of the people.

core_ideas.concept: First-Past-the-Post vs Proportional Representation
core_ideas.explanation: Under first-past-the-post, a party can win 35% of the votes and 80% of the seats, or swing from power to nowhere on small shifts in vote share. Proportional representation gives seats in proportion to votes, so smaller parties and minority interests get a voice in Parliament. Amit avoids taking a side, noting that wise people disagree. His larger point is that elections alone don't make a democracy: a republic also needs rules of the game.
core_ideas.quote: First past the post means that a party with thirty-five percent of the votes can actually have eighty percent of the seats. It is entirely possible.

core_ideas.concept: Tactical Voting Hides True Preferences
core_ideas.explanation: Voters often back the candidate who can beat the one they dislike most, rather than the one they actually prefer. Amit cites Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem to argue that a political marketplace cannot fully satisfy people's true preferences.
core_ideas.quote: Are people's true preferences being revealed? In fact, it is impossible for people's true preferences to be satisfied in a political marketplace.

core_ideas.concept: Booth-Level Results Enable Collective Punishment
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay points out that results are visible booth by booth, and a booth covers about 2,000 people. A winning party therefore knows how each basti voted and can reward or punish the whole community. He calls this a fundamental negation of liberal democracy, and a key enabler of vote-buying.
core_ideas.quote: because the voting outcome is visible one booth at a time and a booth is two thousand people, then the winning party is able to have that reciprocity of carrot and stick against that basti

core_ideas.concept: The Rules of the Game Matter Most
core_ideas.explanation: Incentives come from how the state is designed, and the constitution sets the rules of the game. A good constitution limits the state and protects citizens. The test of a good system is whether a terrible person could gain power and still do little harm, because the state simply doesn't have that much power. Buchanan and Tullock argued that a constitution should contain only what everyone agrees on.
core_ideas.quote: the best system that I can think of is a system in which the worst person in the world, and Adolf Hitler even, can get to power and not manage to do any damage because he or she simply doesn't have that much power.

core_ideas.concept: India's Constitution Protects the State More Than the Citizen
core_ideas.explanation: The Constitution was written when the country was falling apart and it was unclear whether the princely states would join. For understandable reasons, it centralised power and copied the colonial setup in which the state rules and the people are subjects. Free speech gets lip service but is hedged by caveats such as public order and decency. Amit sees a dilemma: the Constitution is less liberal than he would like but more liberal than Indian society. Every government since Nehru has amended it whenever it wanted to do something unconstitutional.
core_ideas.quote: So you have a relatively liberal constitution imposed on an illiberal society by a bunch of unelected people.

core_ideas.concept: Constitutions Are Elite Projects
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that successful constitutions rarely reflect broad consensus. They are written by elites at a 'constitutional moment', and the German and Japanese ones were partly imposed by an outside power. In India, the real constitution is effectively the basic structure, which the judiciary has mostly though not always defended against amendments. The rest functions like an ordinary law that keeps getting amended. That pushes India toward something like the British unwritten tradition, where the work lies in wisely applying the basic structure doctrine.
core_ideas.quote: There is actually a constitution which is the basic structure where by and large the judiciary has been defending it against amendments, sometimes though not always. And the rest of the constitution is like one more parliamentary law and it keeps getting amended all the time.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit claims to have written the first public choice limerick ever, for his weekly Times of India slot: 'A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, / we steal people's money / and use some of it to buy their votes.'
Ajay: 'This is even before ChatGPT?' Amit: ChatGPT 'can't write limericks because it can't count, it can't do math', and a good limerick needs a 9-9-6-6-9 syllable count, not just rhymes.

Amit's rent-seeking hypothetical: the government decides people like Amit Varma and Ajay Shah can't podcast without a licence, 'renewable every six months. And of course I have to pay a bribe for it.'

Amit sets Ajay a quiz on what Raees has to do with public choice theory. Ajay doesn't know and hasn't seen the film. Amit: 'Good.' His verdict on the plot: SRK's bootlegger should be backing the prohibitionist politician: 'Yatra karo, I will dance at your wedding also.'

Quote duel: Ajay cites PJ O'Rourke ('giving money and power to politicians is like giving whiskey and car keys to teenagers'). Amit replies: 'You throw a PJ O'Rourke quote at me, I will raise you with HL Mencken': every election is 'a sort of an advanced auction sale of stolen goods.'
Amit on what Indian elections really decide: 'I really think of the elections as a battle to be the one legal mafia for five years.'
Ajay on why Indians think corruption means suitcases of cash: 'I blame Bollywood for this.'
Listing the many voices that should matter in a liberal democracy (journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs), Ajay adds: 'Podcasters should matter. Podcasters should matter above all.'

Ajay calls elections 'the great temple of the Amar Chitra Katha version of democracy', where the people vote and all problems are solved. Amit replies that first he wants to talk about 'the great temple of Indian entertainment, which is Bollywood.'
Amit says people signal left turns even on an empty road because it is a habit, 'unless you're in Bombay and you drive like me.'
Ajay's confession: 'I am very sad to say, but I have not voted because I never felt the cost benefit analysis made sense and it has been a mystery to me why people vote.'
Amit recalls an old cartoon: someone asks the Parliament bookshop for the Constitution and is told, 'we only stock books here, not periodicals.'

Ajay on India's constitutional moment: 'some people wrote a United States Constitution, some people wrote the Constitution of India, and we lucked out and got a fairly bad document.' Earlier, Amit corrected him mid-sentence: 'Elite rather than elitist.'
Ajay: 'There's no Mahalanobis and Nehru anymore. Nobody is dreaming what the country wants to be.' Amit: 'And in a sense, thank God that's gone.'
Mai Baap Sarkar: Amit's name for India's 'religion of government', the belief that a parental state should solve every problem.
The two wolves and a sheep cartoon: majority voting on what to have for dinner, used as Amit's image of the dangers of democracy.
Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem, which Amit cites to argue that a political marketplace can't satisfy people's true preferences.
